title: Goniometry
keywords: goniometer goniometry rom range of motion joint angle measurement aaom aaos end feel naapna
summary: Measure joint range like an expert: landmarks, axis and arm alignment, normal ranges, end-feels and substitutions for 39 joint motions — with a drag-the-goniometer trainer.
ur: Joint ki range ko goniometer se sahi measure karna — axis, arms, normal values, end-feel aur common mistakes ke saath.

sources.title: Norkin & White — Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry (5th ed.)
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) — Joint Motion: Method of Measuring and Recording

goals.beginner: Know the goniometer, the 0–180 system and normal ranges.
goals.intermediate: Place the axis and arms correctly for every major joint.
goals.advanced: Recognise end-feels, capsular patterns and measurement errors.
goals.expert: Interpret limitation, track meaningful change and report like a specialist.

concepts.title: What goniometry measures
concepts.body: Goniometry measures the **angle a joint moves through**. It turns “the knee is stiff” into “knee flexion 0–95°” — a number you can compare between sides, between visits and with normal values.
bullets: **AROM** — the patient moves; shows willingness, strength and coordination.
**PROM** — you move the joint; shows joint and soft-tissue mobility.
Always record which one you measured.
concepts.ur: Goniometry se joint movement ka angle measure karte hain — taake 'stiff' likhne ki jagah exact number likh saken.

concepts.title: Know your goniometer
concepts.body: A universal goniometer has a **body** (a protractor with the **axis/fulcrum** at its centre), a **stationary arm** fixed to the body and a **moving arm** that rotates and points to the scale.
bullets: Large (12-inch) for big joints, small/finger goniometers for the hand.
Inclinometers and CROM devices for the spine; tape measure for spinal flexion and TMJ.

demo.axis: Lateral femoral epicondyle

concepts.title: The 0–180 system
concepts.body: The anatomical position is **0°** for almost every joint; movement is measured away from it. Record the **start and end** values: “knee flexion 0–135°”. A knee that cannot fully straighten is recorded as “10–135°” — it lacks 10° of extension.
concepts.ur: Anatomical position = 0°. Start aur end dono likhein, jaise 0–135°.

concepts.title: Six steps for every measurement
concepts.body: Good goniometry is a routine, not a guess.
bullets: **Position** the patient in the standard test position.
**Align** the axis, stationary arm and moving arm.
**Move and measure** at the end of range (realign before reading).
**Record** joint, motion, AROM/PROM, values, position and pain.

concepts.title: Normal values are a guide
concepts.body: Normal ranges change with **age, sex, body type and the textbook**. AAOS values are a common reference. The patient's **other side** is often the best normal — and function matters more than the number.

concepts.title: Arms matter more than the axis
concepts.body: The axis is only an approximation of the joint's moving axis. Accurate readings come from aligning the **arms along the bony landmarks** — then the axis falls where it needs to be.
bullets: Keep the goniometer flat against the limb without pressing into soft tissue.
Re-check the alignment at the end of range before reading.

concepts.title: Reading the scale correctly
concepts.body: Goniometers have two scales running in opposite directions. Read the one that started at 0, look at the scale **straight on** (avoid parallax) and remember the joints whose start reading is not 0.

concepts.title: Stabilise to stop false range
concepts.body: Substitution adds degrees that are not there: the back arching during shoulder flexion, the pelvis tilting during hip flexion, the foot rolling in during dorsiflexion. Stabilise the proximal segment and watch neighbouring joints.

concepts.title: Recording hypomobility and hypermobility
concepts.body: Write the full arc. **“R elbow flexion 15–120° (PROM), pain at end range”** says the elbow lacks 15° extension and 30° flexion. Hyperextension is recorded as extra range past 0: “elbow 0–10° hyperextension, 0–150° flexion”. Some clinics use the SFTR notation — follow your setting.

concepts.title: End-feel: what stops the movement
concepts.body: At the end of PROM, apply gentle overpressure and feel the barrier.

head: End-feel
Normal example
Pathological when…
rows: Felt earlier than expected — oedema, synovitis
Occurs early with reduced range — capsular tightness
Pain stops movement before tissue resistance — acute inflammation, serious pathology
Rebound — torn meniscus or loose body

concepts.title: Capsular patterns
concepts.body: Arthritis or capsulitis limits a joint in a predictable order (Cyriax).

head: Joint
Capsular pattern (most → least limited)
rows: Lateral flexion and rotation equally > extension

concepts.title: Two-joint muscles change the reading
concepts.body: Keep two-joint muscles slack when measuring **joint** range: hip flexion with the knee bent (hamstrings), ankle dorsiflexion with the knee bent (gastrocnemius), wrist movements with the fingers relaxed. Measuring with the muscle stretched is a **muscle-length** test instead.

concepts.title: How accurate is a goniometer?
concepts.body: Same tester, same position, same landmarks: reliability is good (often within about 5°). Between testers it is lower. A change smaller than the measurement error — roughly **5° for most limb joints** — may not be real. Spinal goniometry is the least reliable; inclinometers and tape methods are preferred.

concepts.title: Interpreting a limitation
concepts.body: Ask what limits the range and whether it matters.
bullets: **AROM < PROM** — weakness, pain or poor control; **AROM = PROM, both low** — stiffness.
**Capsular pattern + firm early end-feel** — joint capsule; **non-capsular** — ligament, loose body, extra-articular cause.
**Painful arc** — impingement or tendinopathy; **empty end-feel** — stop and screen for red flags.
Compare with **functional ranges**: elbow 30–130°, forearm 50°/50°, knee 90–105° to rise from a chair.

concepts.title: Tracking meaningful change
concepts.body: Use the same position, landmarks, instrument and (ideally) tester at every visit; note pain, time of day and whether you warmed the tissue up. Treat changes larger than the measurement error as real. Link progress to goals: “knee flexion 85° → 105°; now rises from a standard chair without hands.”

stations.title: Measure knee flexion PROM
stations.scenario: A patient is 6 weeks after an ACL reconstruction. Measure right knee flexion passive range and report it.
tasks: Palpate landmarks and align the goniometer.
Measure PROM and record the arc.
checklist: Explains the procedure and checks pain
Supine, hip allowed to flex as the knee bends
Palpates the lateral femoral epicondyle, greater trochanter and lateral malleolus
Axis on the lateral epicondyle; stationary arm toward the greater trochanter; moving arm along the fibula to the lateral malleolus
Stabilises the femur and prevents hip rotation
Re-aligns at end range and reads the correct scale
Records side, PROM, full arc and end-feel (e.g. R knee flexion PROM 0–110°, firm)

stations.title: Measure shoulder abduction AROM

checklist: Supine, palm up (external rotation) and elbow extended
Axis on the anterior acromion
Stationary arm parallel to the sternum; moving arm along the anterior humerus to the medial epicondyle
Stabilises the thorax and watches for lateral trunk lean and shrugging
Reads at end range after re-aligning
Reports range and any painful arc

Measure DF with the knee extended.
checklist: Axis at the lateral malleolus
Stationary arm along the fibula to the fibular head; moving arm parallel to the 5th metatarsal
Records the change from the 90° start reading
Keeps the subtalar joint neutral (no rolling in)
Measures in both knee positions
Interprets less DF with the knee straight as gastrocnemius tightness

stations.title: Lumbar flexion: modified-modified Schober
stations.scenario: A 28-year-old with inflammatory-type back pain. Measure lumbar flexion with the modified-modified Schober test.
tasks: Measure in standing and full flexion.
checklist: Locates the PSISs and marks the midline between them
Marks a point 15 cm above
Asks for maximal forward bending with knees straight
Measures the new distance with the tape following the skin
Calculates the increase and interprets (< about 5 cm = restricted)

cards.back: Soft (thigh against abdomen) or firm (posterior capsule, gluteus maximus)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip flexion?
cards.back: Posterior pelvic tilt (lumbar flexion) adds false range — watch the ASIS and opposite thigh.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Hip extension?
Patient position for measuring Hip extension?
cards.back: Prone, both hips 0°, knee of the tested leg extended (no pillow under the abdomen).

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Hip extension?
cards.back: Lateral aspect of the hip over the greater trochanter

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Hip extension?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the pelvis

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Hip extension?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the femur toward the lateral epicondyle

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Hip extension?
cards.back: Pelvis — prevent anterior tilt and rotation.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Hip extension?
cards.back: Firm (anterior capsule, iliofemoral ligament, hip flexors)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip extension?
cards.back: Lumbar extension/anterior pelvic tilt inflates the reading; knee flexion tightens rectus femoris.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Hip abduction?
Patient position for measuring Hip abduction?
cards.back: Supine, hip and knee 0°, pelvis level.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Hip abduction?
cards.back: Over the ASIS of the tested side

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Hip abduction?
cards.back: Along the line between the two ASISs

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Hip abduction?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the femur toward the middle of the patella

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Hip abduction?
cards.back: Pelvis (opposite ASIS) — prevent lateral tilt and hip hiking.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Hip abduction?
cards.back: Firm (medial capsule, adductors)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip abduction?
cards.back: The goniometer reads 90° at the start — record the change (0–45°); pelvic hiking and external rotation add range.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Hip adduction?
Patient position for measuring Hip adduction?
cards.back: Supine, opposite leg abducted to make room; tested hip and knee 0°.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Hip adduction?
cards.back: Over the ASIS of the tested side

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Hip adduction?
cards.back: Along the line between the two ASISs

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Hip adduction?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the femur toward the middle of the patella

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Hip adduction?
cards.back: Pelvis — prevent lateral tilt.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Hip adduction?
cards.back: Firm (lateral capsule, iliotibial band, abductors)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip adduction?
cards.back: Forgetting to move the other leg out of the way; internal rotation creeping in.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Hip internal rotation?
Patient position for measuring Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Sitting, hip and knee at 90°, towel under the distal thigh; the foot swings outward as the hip rotates in.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Anterior aspect of the patella

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Perpendicular to the floor (vertical)

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the tibia toward the midpoint between the malleoli

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Distal femur — prevent hip adduction and the pelvis lifting.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: Firm (posterior capsule, ischiofemoral ligament, external rotators)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip internal rotation?
cards.back: The pelvis lifting on the tested side or trunk lean; confusing the direction (foot moves out = internal rotation).

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Hip external rotation?
Patient position for measuring Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Sitting, hip and knee at 90°; the foot swings inward as the hip rotates out.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Anterior aspect of the patella

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Perpendicular to the floor (vertical)

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the tibia toward the midpoint between the malleoli

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Distal femur — prevent hip abduction and the pelvis lifting.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Firm (anterior capsule, iliofemoral and pubofemoral ligaments)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Hip external rotation?
cards.back: Lifting the opposite side of the pelvis and lateral trunk flexion.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Knee flexion?
Patient position for measuring Knee flexion?
cards.back: Supine, knee extended; the hip flexes as the knee bends (so rectus femoris doesn't limit range).

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Knee flexion?
cards.back: Lateral epicondyle of the femur

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Knee flexion?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the femur toward the greater trochanter

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Knee flexion?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the fibula toward the lateral malleolus

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Knee flexion?
cards.back: Femur — prevent hip rotation and abduction.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Knee flexion?
cards.back: Soft (calf against thigh) or firm (rectus femoris tension if the hip is extended)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Knee flexion?
cards.back: Measuring in prone with the hip extended (rectus femoris limits range); the goniometer drifting off the fibular line.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Ankle dorsiflexion?
Patient position for measuring Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Sitting with the knee flexed at least 30° (slackens gastrocnemius), ankle 0° inversion/eversion.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Lateral malleolus

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the fibula toward the fibular head

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Parallel to the lateral aspect of the 5th metatarsal

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Tibia and fibula.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: Firm (posterior capsule, Achilles tendon, soleus)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Ankle dorsiflexion?
cards.back: The goniometer reads 90° at the start — record the change; subtalar pronation (foot rolling in) falsely adds range.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Ankle plantarflexion?
Patient position for measuring Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Sitting with the knee flexed at least 30°, ankle 0° inversion/eversion.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Lateral malleolus

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Lateral midline of the fibula toward the fibular head

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Parallel to the lateral aspect of the 5th metatarsal

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Tibia and fibula.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Firm (anterior capsule, tibialis anterior) or hard (talus on tibia)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Ankle plantarflexion?
cards.back: Toe flexion and inversion mixed into the movement.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Foot inversion (tarsal)?
Patient position for measuring Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Sitting, knee flexed 90°, ankle 0°.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior ankle, midway between the malleoli

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the lower leg toward the tibial tuberosity

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the 2nd metatarsal

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Tibia and fibula — prevent hip rotation and knee extension.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Firm (lateral ligaments, capsule, peronei)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Foot inversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Hip external rotation and plantarflexion substituting.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Foot eversion (tarsal)?
Patient position for measuring Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Sitting, knee flexed 90°, ankle 0°.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior ankle, midway between the malleoli

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the lower leg toward the tibial tuberosity

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Anterior midline of the 2nd metatarsal

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Tibia and fibula — prevent hip rotation.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Hard (calcaneus on talus) or firm (deltoid ligament, tibialis posterior)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Foot eversion (tarsal)?
cards.back: Hip internal rotation and dorsiflexion substituting.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Great toe MTP extension?
Patient position for measuring Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Supine or sitting, ankle and foot 0°, first MTP 0° abduction.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Medial aspect of the first MTP joint (or dorsal)

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Medial midline of the 1st metatarsal

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Medial midline of the proximal phalanx

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: First metatarsal.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Firm (plantar capsule, plantar fascia, flexor hallucis brevis)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Great toe MTP extension?
cards.back: Ankle plantarflexion allowing more toe extension.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Great toe MTP flexion?
Patient position for measuring Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Supine or sitting, ankle and foot 0°.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Medial aspect of the first MTP joint (or dorsal)

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Medial midline of the 1st metatarsal

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Medial midline of the proximal phalanx

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: First metatarsal.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Firm (dorsal capsule, extensor hallucis brevis)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Great toe MTP flexion?
cards.back: Ankle dorsiflexion during the movement.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Cervical flexion?
Patient position for measuring Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Sitting, back supported, thoracic and lumbar spine well supported; head in neutral.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Over the external auditory meatus

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Perpendicular or parallel to the floor

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Aligned with the base of the nares

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Shoulder girdle and trunk — prevent thoracic flexion.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Firm (posterior ligaments and muscles)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Cervical flexion?
cards.back: Trunk flexion and forward head shifting; CROM device or tape measure (chin-to-sternum) are more reliable.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Cervical extension?
Patient position for measuring Cervical extension?
cards.back: Sitting, trunk supported, head neutral.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Cervical extension?
cards.back: Over the external auditory meatus

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Cervical extension?
cards.back: Perpendicular or parallel to the floor

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Cervical extension?
cards.back: Aligned with the base of the nares

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Cervical extension?
cards.back: Shoulder girdle and trunk — prevent thoracic extension.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Cervical extension?
cards.back: Firm (anterior ligaments and muscles)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Cervical extension?
cards.back: Thoracic extension/leaning back. Stop if dizziness or visual symptoms appear.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Cervical lateral flexion?
Patient position for measuring Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Sitting, trunk supported, head neutral.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Over the spinous process of C7

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Along the thoracic spinous processes (perpendicular to the floor)

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Dorsal midline of the head toward the occipital protuberance

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Shoulder girdle — prevent lateral trunk flexion and shoulder elevation.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Firm (ligaments and opposite-side muscles)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Cervical lateral flexion?
cards.back: Shoulder elevation toward the ear and rotation mixed in.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Cervical rotation?
Patient position for measuring Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Supine (or sitting), head neutral.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Centre of the cranial (top) aspect of the head

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Parallel to the line between the two acromial processes

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Aligned with the tip of the nose

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Shoulder girdle — prevent trunk rotation.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Firm (ligaments, opposite rotators)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Cervical rotation?
cards.back: Starting reading is 90° — record the change; lateral flexion mixed in. CROM devices often show 70–80°.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
Patient position for measuring Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Standing, feet shoulder-width apart, weight equal.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Over the posterior aspect of the S1 spinous process

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Perpendicular to the ground

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Toward the C7 spinous process

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Pelvis — prevent lateral tilt and hip/knee flexion.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Firm (ligaments and opposite-side muscles)

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Thoracolumbar lateral flexion?
cards.back: Trunk flexion or rotation; lifting the heel or bending the knee. Fingertip-to-floor distance is an alternative.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Thoracolumbar rotation?
Patient position for measuring Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Sitting (stabilises the pelvis), feet on the floor.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Centre of the cranial (top) aspect of the head

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Parallel to the line between the iliac crests

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Parallel to the line between the acromial processes

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Pelvis.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Firm

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Thoracolumbar rotation?
cards.back: Cervical rotation added to the movement; the pelvis turning.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Increase of about 5 cm or more (healthy adults commonly 6–7 cm)

cards.front: Patient position for measuring Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Standing, feet shoulder-width apart; mark the midline between the PSISs (S2 level) and a point 15 cm above.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Not a goniometer test — use a tape measure

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Mark 1: midline at the level of the PSISs

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Mark 2: 15 cm above mark 1

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: None — the patient bends forward as far as possible with knees straight.

cards.front: Normal end-feel for Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Firm

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober?
cards.back: Marking the wrong level and letting the knees bend; the tape must follow the skin.

cards.front: Normal range (AAOS) for TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: About 35–50 mm (functional ≥ 35 mm, roughly three knuckles)

cards.front: Patient position for measuring TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Sitting, head neutral, teeth together at the start.

cards.front: Where do you place the goniometer axis for TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Not a goniometer test — use a ruler

cards.front: Alignment of the stationary arm for TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Incisal edge of an upper central incisor

cards.front: Alignment of the moving arm for TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Incisal edge of the lower central incisor

cards.front: What do you stabilise when measuring TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Head (avoid neck extension).

cards.front: Normal end-feel for TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Firm

cards.front: Common error or substitution when measuring TMJ mouth opening?
cards.back: Neck extension while opening; ignoring deviation (S-curve) or deflection of the jaw.

cards.front: A knee is recorded as “10–120°”. What does this tell you?
cards.back: It lacks 10° of extension and flexes to 120°. The arc starts at 10° instead of 0°, so full extension is missing by 10°.

cards.front: Which part of the goniometer is placed over the joint?
cards.back: The axis (fulcrum). The axis sits over the approximate joint axis; the arms align with the segments.

cards.front: PROM is measured when…
cards.back: The examiner moves the joint. Passive range = examiner moves the relaxed joint.

cards.front: Starting position for most goniometric measurements is…
cards.back: Anatomical position = 0°. The 0–180 system starts from the anatomical position.

cards.front: The best ‘normal’ to compare with is often…
cards.back: The patient's other side. Normal values vary; the uninjured side reflects that person's normal.

cards.front: Which instrument suits lumbar flexion best?
cards.back: Tape measure (modified-modified Schober). Spinal flexion is measured more reliably with tape or inclinometer methods.

cards.front: For accurate readings, the most important alignment is…
cards.back: The arms along the bony landmarks. Arm alignment along landmarks matters more than exact axis placement.

cards.front: Hip abduction: at the start the goniometer reads 90°. At end range it reads 130°. Record:
cards.back: 0–40°. Hip abduction starts at a 90° reading — record the change (130 − 90 = 40°).

cards.front: During shoulder flexion in supine, the patient arches the back. Effect?
cards.back: False extra flexion is recorded. Lumbar extension adds apparent shoulder flexion — flatten the back with knees bent.

cards.front: Why measure knee flexion in supine with the hip flexing?
cards.back: So rectus femoris doesn't limit knee flexion. With the hip extended, rectus femoris tension can stop knee flexion early.

cards.front: Ankle dorsiflexion is normally measured with the knee…
cards.back: Flexed at least 30°. Knee flexion slackens gastrocnemius so true talocrural range is measured.

cards.front: Where is the axis for forearm pronation?
cards.back: Lateral and proximal to the ulnar styloid. The axis sits just lateral and proximal to the ulnar styloid; the moving arm crosses the dorsal forearm.

cards.front: Correct documentation:
cards.back: L knee flexion PROM 5–110°, supine, pain at end range. Side, motion, AROM/PROM, full arc, position and pain.

cards.front: Normal end-feel of elbow extension?
cards.back: Hard (olecranon in fossa). Bone-on-bone contact gives a hard end-feel at full elbow extension.

cards.front: An ‘empty’ end-feel means…
cards.back: Pain stops movement before tissue resistance is felt — always abnormal. Empty end-feel suggests acute inflammation, bursitis or serious pathology.

cards.front: Shoulder capsular pattern?
cards.back: External rotation > abduction > internal rotation. Frozen shoulder and glenohumeral arthritis limit ER most.

cards.front: A springy block at the end of knee extension suggests…
cards.back: A torn meniscus or loose body. A rebound feel suggests an internal derangement.

cards.front: A change of 3° in shoulder ER between two visits most likely…
cards.back: Falls within measurement error. Changes smaller than about 5° may reflect measurement error.

cards.front: Measuring hip flexion with the knee straight mainly tests…
cards.back: Hamstring length. A straight knee puts the hamstrings on stretch — that is the SLR/hamstring length test.

cards.front: A 52-year-old with shoulder pain for 3 months: PROM ER 20°, abduction 80°, IR 50°; firm early end-feel; AROM = PROM. — Most likely interpretation?
cards.back: Capsular pattern — adhesive capsulitis or GH arthritis. ER > abduction > IR limitation with firm end-feel and AROM = PROM fits a capsular lesion.

cards.front: After knee replacement: AROM 15–80°, PROM 5–95°. — What does the AROM/PROM gap suggest?
cards.back: Quadriceps lag/weakness and pain limit active range. When PROM exceeds AROM, the limitation is partly muscular (extension lag) or pain-related.

cards.front: A patient can't rise from a standard chair without using the hands. Knee flexion PROM is 85°. — What target would help this goal?
cards.back: About 90–105° of knee flexion. Rising from a standard chair typically needs about 90–105° of knee flexion.

cards.front: Ankle dorsiflexion: 15° with the knee bent, 0° with the knee straight. — Which tissue is limiting?
cards.back: Gastrocnemius. Losing range only when the knee is straight implicates the two-joint gastrocnemius.

cards.front: Hip pain in a 60-year-old: hip IR 10°, flexion 95°, abduction 30°; firm end-feel. — What does this pattern suggest?
cards.back: Hip osteoarthritis (capsular pattern). Early loss of internal rotation then flexion and abduction fits the hip capsular pattern.

cards.front: Elbow: AROM 30–110°, PROM 30–115°, hard end-feel at 30° extension two years after a supracondylar fracture. — What limits extension?
cards.back: A bony block (malunion/osteophyte). An early hard end-feel at the same point actively and passively suggests bone, not soft tissue.

cards.front: Wrist extension 40° with the fingers relaxed but 20° with the fingers fully straight. — What is limiting wrist extension with the fingers straight?
cards.back: Length of the long finger flexors. Two-joint finger flexors tighten when fingers and wrist extend together.

cards.front: A footballer with a 'stiff big toe': 1st MTP extension 25°, painful dorsal bump. — Which functional task will be most affected?
cards.back: Push-off/toe-off in walking and running. Toe-off needs about 60° of 1st MTP extension; hallux rigidus limits push-off.

cards.front: Cervical rotation 40° to the right and 70° to the left; extension reproduces arm pain on the right. — What should you add next?
cards.back: Neurological examination (dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes) of the right arm. Asymmetric rotation with arm pain on extension suggests foraminal involvement — screen for radiculopathy.

cards.front: Which practice best improves repeated-measurement reliability?
cards.back: Same tester, position, landmarks and instrument each visit. Standardisation reduces error so you can trust change over time.

cards.front: Shoulder flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: About 120° of flexion is enough for most daily activities; overhead work and sport need the full range.

cards.front: Shoulder external rotation — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: External rotation is the first and most limited motion in the shoulder capsular pattern (frozen shoulder).

cards.front: Elbow flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Most daily activities need about 30–130° of elbow flexion (Morrey).

cards.front: Forearm pronation — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Daily tasks need roughly 50° of pronation and 50° of supination.

cards.front: Wrist extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Functional activities use about 35–40° of wrist extension.

cards.front: Hip flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A straight knee limits hip flexion by hamstring tension — that is a muscle-length test, not joint ROM.

cards.front: Hip extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Other sources report 10–20°; compare sides.

cards.front: Hip internal rotation — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Hip internal rotation is usually the first motion lost in hip osteoarthritis.

cards.front: Knee flexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Functional knee flexion: about 60–70° for walking, 85–100° for stairs and 90–105° to rise from a chair.

cards.front: Ankle dorsiflexion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Measure with the knee flexed and extended: less dorsiflexion with the knee straight = tight gastrocnemius.

cards.front: Great toe MTP extension — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Normal walking needs about 60° of first MTP extension at toe-off; hallux rigidus limits it.

cards.front: Lumbar flexion — modified-modified Schober — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: An increase below about 5 cm suggests restricted lumbar flexion (used in ankylosing spondylitis screening, e.g. BASMI).
